hints: Notice the $v$ value at each marked point: rest means $v = 0$ where the curve meets the $t$-axis at R, not the peak at Q.
Recall acceleration on a $v$-$t$ graph is the gradient $a = dv/dt$, so look for where the tangent is flat versus steep.
Compare the tangents: P slopes steeply up, Q is flat at the top, and R slopes steeply down through zero - decide which gives zero gradient.
walkthrough: Read the axes: vertical is velocity $v$ and horizontal is time $t$, with points P on the rise, Q at the peak, and R where the curve crosses the $t$-axis.
Momentarily at rest means $v = 0$. Only R lies on $v = 0$; at P and Q the $v$ value is positive and large.
Acceleration is the gradient of a $v$-$t$ graph, $a = dv/dt$. A steep slope means large acceleration and a flat tangent means zero acceleration.
At P the tangent slopes steeply upward so $a$ is positive. At R the tangent slopes steeply downward so $a$ is negative and large.
At Q the curve turns over at maximum $v$, so the tangent is horizontal and $dv/dt = 0$, giving zero acceleration.
Thus rest is R and zero acceleration is Q. This is option C.

options.A: Q is the peak where $v$ is maximum, not zero, and P is on a steep rising section so the gradient and acceleration are not zero.
options.B: Q has maximum $v$ so the jumper is not at rest, and R is on a steep falling section so the $v$-$t$ gradient and acceleration are non-zero.
options.C: R is where the curve crosses $v = 0$ so the jumper is momentarily at rest, and Q is the peak with horizontal tangent so gradient $a = dv/dt = 0$.
options.D: R correctly gives $v = 0$ for rest, but at R the graph is steepest downward so the magnitude of acceleration is large, not zero.
